subject: Civil Engineering
title: Constructed Wetlands
description: A quick, practical guide to Constructed Wetlands.

hook.text: A marsh can clean water as well as a treatment plant — nature's own filter.

buildup.text: Constructed wetlands route wastewater through beds of gravel planted with reeds and cattails.

discovery.text: Plant roots host bacteria that consume nutrients. Gravel filters solids. Sunlight kills pathogens.

twist.text: They need no electricity, no chemicals, and minimal maintenance — perfect for rural areas.

climax.text: The town of Arcata, California, treats its sewage in a constructed wetland that doubles as a bird sanctuary.

punchline.text: Build a wetland and nature treats the sewage for free.

quiz.question: What advantage do constructed wetlands have over conventional treatment plants?
options: They process wastewater faster than mechanical treatment
They require no electricity, no chemicals, and minimal maintenance
They can handle unlimited volumes of industrial wastewater

details.summary: Constructed wetlands treat wastewater using natural processes of filtration, sedimentation, microbial decomposition, and plant uptake in engineered shallow basins planted with emergent vegetation like reeds and bulrushes.
details.whyItMatters: Constructed wetlands treat wastewater without pumps, chemicals, or skilled operators, making them ideal for developing communities and rural areas where conventional treatment plants are unaffordable to build and operate.
takeaways: Subsurface flow wetlands pass wastewater through a gravel bed planted with emergent vegetation
Wetlands achieve 80-95% removal of suspended solids and biochemical oxygen demand
Operating costs are 10-20% of conventional treatment plants of equivalent capacity

faq.question: How do constructed wetlands treat wastewater without mechanical equipment?
faq.answer: Wastewater flows slowly through gravel beds where biofilm on gravel surfaces and plant roots decomposes organic matter. Plant roots transport oxygen into the bed, supporting aerobic bacteria. Particles settle and are filtered by the gravel matrix. Plants take up nutrients.

faq.question: What are the limitations of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment?
faq.answer: They require large land areas, typically 5-10 square meters per person equivalent. Performance decreases in cold climates when biological activity slows. Nutrient removal, particularly nitrogen, requires careful design of aerobic and anaerobic zones.
